    Tokenization in practice: padding, truncation, packing

    After this lesson you can configure max sequence length sensibly, explain padding and attention masks, use sequence packing, and avoid truncation silently dropping your completions.

    Level: beginner Read time: ~10 min Prerequisites: Task shapes: classification, QA, extraction, summarization, chat Verified: 12 Nov 2026

    You met tokenization in Track 0: text → subword tokens → IDs → embeddings. Training adds a handful of practical mechanics that, done wrong, quietly corrupt your data. None are hard; all are worth getting right.

    Padding and the attention mask

    The GPU processes a batch of sequences at once, and a batch must be rectangular — every row the same length. Real examples vary in length, so shorter ones are padded with a special pad token up to the batch's longest. To stop the model from treating padding as real content, each example carries an attention mask: a 1 for real tokens, 0 for padding, telling attention to ignore the padded positions. As long as padded positions are masked in both the attention mask and the labels (label -100, so the loss ignores them), padding affects only batching efficiency, never the meaning.

    Truncation and max_seq_length

    max_seq_length caps how many tokens an example may have. Anything longer is truncated — cut to fit. This is where a real bug hides: if you truncate from the end, you can chop off the completion (the part you actually train on), leaving the model nothing to learn. It's also the default: TRL's SFTTrainer truncates every example to max_length=1024 tokens with truncation_mode="keep_start" (the only mode current TRL supports), so a long example loses its end — which is where the completion sits. Choose max_seq_length (TRL: max_length) from your data's actual length distribution, and when you must shorten an example, cut the prompt/context yourself before formatting, or drop the row, so the completion survives.

    Silent data bug

    Truncation that clips completions lets training run normally while teaching the model partial or empty targets. Always inspect your token-length distribution and confirm completions fit before a long run.

    Sequence packing

    If your examples are short and max_seq_length is large, most of each padded sequence is wasted compute. Sequence packing concatenates several short examples into one full-length sequence, so the GPU does useful work instead of multiplying padding. It needs care: examples shouldn't "attend across" each other, and position counting should restart at each boundary. Good packers do both — they reset position IDs per example and use an attention kernel that respects the boundaries (TRL's default packing strategy, bfd, does this with FlashAttention). Naive concatenate-and-chunk packing doesn't: every example can see the ones before it in the same sequence, which leaks context between unrelated examples. Done right, the payoff is a sizable throughput win on short-example datasets.

    Padding side and cost

    For causal (decoder-only) models, the padding side matters at inference — typically left-padding so the real tokens end at the sequence's end where generation continues. And remember the cost lever: attention compute grows with the square of sequence length, and every other cost grows at least linearly, so a larger max_seq_length is more expensive per step (at typical SFT lengths the feed-forward layers still dominate, and memory-efficient attention kernels keep attention memory linear). Pick the smallest length that comfortably fits your data.

    Key idea

    Set max_seq_length from your data, not a round number: large enough that completions are never clipped, small enough that you're not paying for empty context.

    Recap

    • A batch must be rectangular, so shorter rows are padded; the attention mask hides the padding from attention and label -100 hides it from the loss.
    • Truncation at max_seq_length cuts from the end, which is where the completion sits (TRL defaults to max_length=1024, keep_start); choose the length from your data and shorten the prompt or drop the row yourself.
    • Packing concatenates short examples to save compute and needs position resets and boundary-respecting attention; a larger max_seq_length costs more per step, so pick the smallest that fits.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    Run the script: it formats four rows with SmolLM2's chat template and applies keep-start truncation at a deliberately small max length of 64 tokens. For each row, how many completion tokens survive?

    from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct")
rows = [
    ("Classify: I loved it", "positive"),
    ("Classify: The battery died after two days and support never replied to my three emails.", "negative"),
    ("Summarize: " + "The committee met on Tuesday to review the budget. " * 8,
     "The committee reviewed the budget on Tuesday and approved it without changes after a short discussion."),
    ("Extract the date: Invoice issued 12 March 2024, due in 30 days.",
     '{"issued": "2024-03-12", "due_days": 30}'),
]
MAX = 64
for prompt, answer in rows:
    text = tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
    p = tok(text, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids
    c = tok(answer + "<|im_end|>", add_special_tokens=False).input_ids
    kept = max(0, min(len(c), MAX - len(p)))  # keep_start truncation
    print("prompt", len(p), "completion", len(c), "-> completion tokens kept:", kept)
    Show answer

    Row by row (prompt tokens, completion tokens, completion kept): 36, 2, 2; 48, 2, 2; 115, 18, 0; 54, 26, 10. The summarisation row loses its entire completion because the prompt alone is over 64 tokens, and the JSON row keeps only 10 of 26 tokens, so it would train on half an object. Training would run normally on both. Prompts include SmolLM2's default system prompt, which is why even the short one is 36 tokens.

    Key terms

    Padding
    Filling shorter sequences with a pad token so a batch is rectangular.
    Attention mask
    A 0/1 marker telling the model to ignore padded positions.
    Truncation
    Cutting sequences longer than max_seq_length; truncate the prompt side to protect the completion.
    max_seq_length
    The cap on tokens per example; set it from the data's length distribution.
    Sequence packing
    Concatenating short examples into one full-length sequence to avoid wasted padding compute; good packers keep examples from attending across each other.
    Padding side
    Which end padding is added; causal models often left-pad at inference.
